title: Kirchhoff's voltage law: why the voltages around a loop add to zero
examples: How do voltage drops add up in a series circuit?
How do I get the signs right in KVL?

parts.label: R1
parts.ask: Why is the current the same everywhere in series?

parts.label: R3
parts.ask: Which resistor gets the biggest voltage drop?

explain.say: Walk up a hill and back down to where you started, and your total change in height is zero. Voltage is like height for charge. On the board, a 12 volt battery lifts the charge up, and three resistors in series, 2, 4 and 6 ohms, let it back down. Let's follow one loop round.

draw.text: Kirchhoff's voltage law: why the voltages around a loop add to zero

parts.label: R1
parts.ask: Why is the current the same everywhere in series?

parts.label: R3
parts.ask: Which resistor gets the biggest voltage drop?

explain.say: First the current. In series there is only one path, so the resistances simply add: 2 plus 4 plus 6 makes 12 ohms. Then Ohm's law gives 12 volts over 12 ohms, which is 1 amp, the same current through every part. Will the 6 ohm resistor carry more current than the 2 ohm one?

parts.label: R1
parts.ask: Why is the current the same everywhere in series?

parts.label: R3
parts.ask: Which resistor gets the biggest voltage drop?

explain.say: No, the same 1 amp flows everywhere in a series loop. But the voltage drops differ. Each drop is I times R: 2 volts across R1, 4 volts across R2 and 6 volts across R3. The biggest resistor takes the biggest share. Which resistor drops 4 volts?

parts.label: R1
parts.ask: Why is the current the same everywhere in series?

parts.label: R3
parts.ask: Which resistor gets the biggest voltage drop?

explain.say: R2, yes. Now Kirchhoff's voltage law: go round any closed loop, add the rises and the drops, and you get zero. Here: plus 12 at the battery, then minus 2, minus 4 and minus 6. Back to zero, just like the hill walk. What would the drops add to with a 9 volt battery instead?

parts.label: R1
parts.ask: Why is the current the same everywhere in series?

parts.label: R3
parts.ask: Which resistor gets the biggest voltage drop?

explain.say: Nine volts, always the supply. Look: 0.75 amps flows, and the drops become 1.5, 3 and 4.5 volts. Brilliant. Exam tip: pick a direction round the loop, count a rise as plus and a drop as minus, and stick to it. Kirchhoff's voltage law is simply energy conservation for every coulomb of charge.

faq.a: The algebraic sum of all the voltages around any closed loop is zero. The rises from sources exactly equal the drops across the other parts.

faq.q: Why is the current the same everywhere in series?
faq.a: A series circuit has only one path, so every charge that passes one part must pass all the others. By Kirchhoff's current law nothing can split off.
asks: Is current the same in a series circuit?

faq.q: Which resistor gets the biggest voltage drop?
faq.a: In series the drop is I times R with the same I, so the largest resistance takes the largest share of the voltage.
asks: How is voltage shared in series?

faq.q: What sign convention should I use for KVL?
faq.a: Choose a direction round the loop. Count going from minus to plus through a source as a rise and going through a resistor along the current as a drop, then keep that choice for the whole loop.
asks: How do I get the signs right in KVL?

faq.a: Voltage is energy per unit charge. A charge that goes round a loop and returns to its start must end with the same energy, so all the gains and losses cancel.

facts: Kirchhoff's voltage law is a form of the conservation of energy.
In a series circuit the total resistance is the sum of the individual resistances.

quiz.say: A 24 volt supply feeds a 3 ohm and a 5 ohm resistor in series. What is the voltage across the 5 ohm resistor?
quiz.show: A 24 V supply feeds 3 Ω and 5 Ω in series. What is the voltage across the 5 Ω resistor?
quiz.why: The total is 8 ohms, so the current is 24 over 8, which is 3 amps. Across 5 ohms that drops 3 times 5, which is 15 volts.

wrong.1: 9 volts is the drop across the 3 ohm resistor.
wrong.2: 12 volts would split the supply equally, ignoring the resistances.

quiz.say: Going round a loop, a battery adds 10 volts and one resistor drops 6 volts. What does the only other resistor drop?
quiz.show: Round a loop, a battery adds 10 V and one resistor drops 6 V. What does the only other resistor drop?
quiz.why: The drops must add up to the rise: 10 minus 6 leaves 4 volts.

wrong.1: That adds the rise and the drop instead of balancing them.
wrong.2: Equal drops only happen with equal resistors.
